cards.title: See Widely, Think Wisely: Toward Designing a Generative Multi-agent System to Burst Filter Bubbles
cards.meta: CHI 2024 · doi 10.1145/3613904.3642545 · comparison only, zero credit

rows.value: The cited theory explains precisely why the obvious remedy fails, and the design answers each part of it. Cited work establishes that reading is steered by prior belief, that people avoid information contradicting them, and that this confirmation bias means simply providing diverse viewpoints is not enough; a cited account of levels of processing says deeper semantic processing is what would be required, and a cited boomerang effect warns that pushing a contrary view too hard moves the belief the wrong way, so cited persuasion advice about acknowledging shared beliefs shapes how the agents speak. Cited nudge theory and a cited split between epistemic and social motivation give the two levers, cited work on embodiment says the other side needs a face, and a cited definition of gamification supplies the puzzle and the points.

While reading a social media thread, the reader can open a panel of invented characters with different backgrounds and argue with them, unlocking pieces of a puzzle as they talk to each one and answer questions about what was said. Eighteen people used it in a lab session. The characters and the question set are the vocabulary of perspectives the reader is offered. This card does not refilter the paper.

rows.value: 1 INTRODUCTION: that recommendation narrows what people see, that the three standard responses all work on the supply of information rather than on the reader, and that a model could argue instead of merely showing (PDF pp. 1–3); 2 RELATED WORK: how prior belief steers what gets processed and why contrary information gets dismissed, the nudges available for motivating engagement, and what models can now do as characters (PDF pp. 3–5)

read to prove design operationalization · 3 PROTOTYPE: a three-hour workshop producing three design considerations, then characters with different backgrounds to talk to, suggested replies, a puzzle that fills in as each is engaged, and questions about what was said (PDF pp. 5–7); 4 USER STUDY: eighteen readers of online content platforms working through posts on one topic, talking with the characters, answering the assessment questions, and then interviewed about the experience (PDF pp. 7–9); 5.1 TO 5.3 RESULTS: which perspectives people reached, how the puzzle and the suggested replies shaped where they went, and what the assessment questions did to how they summarised the topic (PDF pp. 8–12); 5.4 RESULTS: how far people went to complete the puzzle, how convincingly the characters played their parts, what the workload scale showed, and what they made of how the feature was reached (PDF pp. 11–13)

The cited theory is unusually precise about what would count as success, and the study measures something else. Confirmation bias, deeper semantic processing and the boomerang effect together say that exposure is not the problem and that changing what someone does with a contrary view is. What gets reported is engagement: how many character avatars each person lit up, how many puzzle pieces they completed, ratings of pleasure and helpfulness, and a workload scale showing no significant burden. Nobody's position on the topic is measured before or after, and nothing tests what was retained. Two observations in the paper cut against the mechanism it claims. The characters were distinct as labels and not as content: participants reported that asking factual questions produced quite similar answers across the agents, and that a delivery worker who was highly knowledgeable about policy seemed unrealistic, so the perspectives on offer were a cast list rather than a set of genuinely different positions. And the load reduction has a price attached: fifty-five per cent of the reader's own turns were made by clicking a suggested reply, which means over half of the person's side of the argument was written for them, in a study whose purpose is to get people to think their way out of a bubble. One participant read the completion map as an obligation rather than a motivation.
